questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: Phytochrome system

Harakeke / NZ flax (Phormium tenax) are long-day plants that naturally flower in summer when day length is greatest. Many New Zealand alpine herbs and cushion plants are short-day plants, flowering during autumn when days shorten.

Commercial growers in Waikato use their understanding of photoperiodism and the phytochrome system to manipulate harakeke flowering so they can supply cut flowers outside the natural season, including during the short days of a New Zealand winter.

Discuss the phytochrome system, and justify why plant growers in New Zealand alter the light and dark periods to make long-day plants, such as harakeke, flower during the New Zealand winter.

In your answer include discussion of:
- a definition of photoperiodism
- the difference between a short-day and long-day plant
- how the phytochrome system influences flowering in long-day plants.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define photoperiodism (the physiological response of an organism to the relative lengths of light and dark periods). Short-day plants flower when the dark period exceeds a critical length. Long-day plants flower when the dark period is shorter than a critical length. The phytochrome system uses Pr and Pfr forms to detect light conditions.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describe short-day plant.
- long-day plant.
- photoperiodism.
- phytochrome system.
- critical day/night length.

For Merit:
- Explain difference between short-day and long-day plant with reference to critical day/night length.
- how Pr and Pfr work.
- critical day/night length — uninterrupted darkness is critical for Pfr to revert to Pr.
- how flowering is caused in a long-day plant.
- how flowering is caused in a short-day plant.
- how plant growers can produce flowers from long-day plants during NZ winters.

For Excellence:
- Provides detailed discussion of the photoperiodic response of flowering in short-day and long-day plants which includes the phytochrome system.
- how plant growers produce harakeke flowers during New Zealand winters, both methods, with justification.
- Method 1: Plants exposed to supplementary lighting to artificially lengthen the day, maintaining Pfr levels above the critical threshold, inducing flower development.
- Method 2: Night interrupted by red light — red light converts inactive Pr to active Pfr, maintaining high Pfr levels and mimicking a long day, allowing the harakeke to flower.
- N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Weka navigation

The weka (Gallirallus australis) is a ground-dwelling rail found across much of New Zealand. Weka are known for their seasonal movements between food sources — they travel considerable distances to reach food sources such as invertebrates and fallen fruit. They use landmarks and magnetic fields as reference cues and combine this with knowledge of the landscape to navigate.

Weka have been observed to maintain consistent daily activity patterns even when housed in windowless aviaries with constant artificial lighting.

Researchers investigated weka navigation by fitting groups of weka with either clear lenses (control), frosted lenses (blocking detailed vision), or small magnets (disrupting magnetic field perception). The birds were released 60 km from their home forest. The results are summarised in the graph above.

Discuss the behaviour of weka during navigation on clear days and overcast days, using the information above.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- a description of diurnal circadian rhythm, linked to the weka's ability to use the Sun as a compass
- the environmental cues weka use to navigate home on clear days and overcast days
- the navigation performance of the different experimental groups compared to the control
- why some weka can still navigate during overcast conditions when the Sun is not visible.

graph.title: Weka Navigation — Percentage Returned Within 14 Days

questions.expectedAnswer: Describe diurnal organism, circadian rhythm with internal biological clock, Sun compass navigation, landmarks, magnetic field detection. Weka use multiple redundant cues for homing.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describe diurnal organism/behaviour.
- circadian rhythm (includes internal biological clock).
- landmarks used by weka for homing.
- sun compass used for homing.
- Earth's magnetic field used for homing.
- olfactory/scent cues used for homing.
- navigation on clear days.
- navigation on overcast days.

For Merit:
- Explain why weka's circadian rhythm is closely linked to its sun compass.
- environmental cues for homing on clear days.
- environmental cues for homing on overcast days.
- navigation of control group.
- navigation of frosted-lens group.
- navigation of magnet-fitted group.
- why weka navigate during overcast conditions.

For Excellence:
- Provides detailed discussion of circadian rhythm and how weka use environmental cues on clear and overcast days to navigate home.
- weka navigation across the different experimental groups and why some weka still navigate on overcast days.
- The circadian rhythm is closely linked to sun compass.
- Sun's position changes throughout the day and weka constantly adjust navigation using their internal clock.
- On overcast days they use magnetic field detection, landmarks, and olfactory cues.
- Frosted-lens weka could still detect light direction and use magnetic fields.
- Magnet-fitted weka lost magnetic cues and on overcast days also lost sun compass, explaining their poor performance.
- Weka use redundant navigation systems so losing one cue does not necessarily prevent homing.
- N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Behaviour in wild dogs

The African wild dog (Lycaon pictus) is a highly social carnivore that lives in groups of 6–20 individuals. The group is composed of closely related individuals and maintains a clear dominance hierarchy.

Agonistic behaviour such as body postures, snapping and posturing (dominant gestures), and growling are used to establish and maintain rank within the group.

Group structure:
- Alpha pair: dominant male and female who are the primary breeders. They lead foraging excursions and make decisions about group movement.
- Scouts: individuals that patrol the territory perimeter and watch for threats, scanning for aerial and ground predators.
- Subordinates: participate in foraging, guard pups at the den, and bring food back for pups and the nursing mother.
- Lowest-ranked individuals: eat last and receive the most submissive pressure from higher-ranked members.

The group forages cooperatively, with scouts providing alarm calls that allow others to forage safely. Adults bring food for pups and for group members that stayed behind to guard the den.

Discuss advantages and disadvantages of hierarchical behaviour in a wild dog group.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms hierarchy and territory, including definitions
- how the hierarchy of the group is maintained
- how and why members of the group demonstrate kin selection
- an advantage and disadvantage of subordinate individuals living in a hierarchy, compared to living alone.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define hierarchy (a ranking system within a social group based on dominance) and territory (a defended area). Kin selection: subordinates assist relatives, ensuring shared alleles are passed on even though they do not breed directly.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describe hierarchy.
- territory.
- kin selection (must state relatedness).
- an example of kin selection.
- an advantage of living in a group.
- a disadvantage of living in a group.

For Merit:
- Explain at least TWO examples of how the group's hierarchy is maintained.
- why members demonstrate kin selection.
- an example of kin selection linked to genetic relatedness.
- an advantage of living in a group linked to increased survival rate.
- a disadvantage of living in a group linked to cost-benefit.

For Excellence:
- Provides detailed discussion of how the group hierarchy is maintained AND why wild dogs demonstrate kin selection to increase reproductive success.
- advantages of subordinate individuals living in a group AND disadvantages.
- Kin selection examples: scout duty — subordinates take turns standing guard, supporting the alpha pair to remain healthy and reproduce, passing on shared genes.
- pup-care — non-breeding members guard and feed pups, investing in survival of shared alleles.
- territorial defence — subordinates risk injury defending territory, helping the alpha pair maintain resources.
- Advantages: scout system greatly reduces predation risk.
- protection in numbers.
- access to shared food resources.
- future opportunity to breed.
- Disadvantages: eat last.
- less food.
- unlikely to breed directly.
- receive more aggression.
- Ultimately subordinates remain because benefits outweigh costs — they have a greater chance of passing on shared alleles by helping genetically close relatives reproduce.
- N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.
